rv.q: The writing is notably warm and compassionate; tate has a nicely poetic sensibility to their prose.
Martin creates a welcoming environment for us to witness this overdue flowering of familial understanding.
QUEEN OF THE NIGHT ultimately feels like it lacks specificity, and the dynamic between a parent and a child who seem diametrically opposed feels utterly familiar.
“Queen of the Night” celebrates the universal father-and-son connection with stunning sincerity.
Victory Gardens uncovers something small but profound underneath the stars.
This work is something we desperately need right now.
Martin directs this production to have emotional weight that has beauty in its subtlety.
And tate's script has real heart in it.

The moments of real substance, a father struggling with the fact he has just been downsized out of a job, guilt over not always being there for his children in the aftermath of a divorce, the self-acceptance of a gay man in the black community, were buried under a lot of superfluous filler.
But travis tate’s drama, with some moments of comedy thrown in to soften the rough edges, isn’t an especially new story.

Sharpley directed by Ken-matt martin on a wonderful set (Sydney Lynne) and a wonderful assortment of props ( Caitlin McCarthy) and sound ( G. Clausen) and lighting (Sim Carpenter and Connor Sale), I found this to be a family picture of an estranged parent and child trying to get it back together.

cn.t: Critics find this father-son reconciliation drama familiar in premise but largely effective in execution, praising its contemporary take on masculinity and family dynamics alongside an immersive forest set, though some note the dialogue avoids deeper confrontation.
